headline: Three-day tech rally stalls as Mideast-driven oil spike hits risk appetite
body: After a three-session run that carried the S&P 500 to roughly 7,757 and the Nasdaq Composite past 26,700 on Wednesday, the tone flipped overnight. Asian markets sold off sharply into Thursday, with Japan, South Korea, and Hong Kong benchmarks each down several percent, and European indices followed lower. U.S. futures pointed down broadly, with the retreat concentrated in technology and semiconductor names rather than spread evenly across the market; Tesla was among the hardest hit in early trading, falling roughly 4-5%. The proximate trigger looks macro rather than company-specific: an escalation in Middle East tensions pushed oil and broader energy prices higher overnight, reviving inflation and borrowing-cost concerns that had largely faded during the recent rally. That shifts the setup from a momentum-driven advance to a more defensive, wait-and-see posture heading into the session.

Layered on top of the geopolitical jolt is an earnings and policy backdrop that was already doing a lot of work. Tesla and Meta reported after Wednesday's close, and futures reaction to those results was mixed-to-negative into the evening, adding to today's cautious tone rather than offsetting it. On policy, the Fed's October 28 decision is now the next scheduled catalyst; prediction markets have moved toward pricing a hold as the more likely outcome, though Chair Warsh has declined to preview the meeting and the odds have swung noticeably over the past few weeks. Retail and social-media chatter didn't surface anything concrete enough to characterize today's crowd positioning with confidence, so this read leans on overnight price action, oil, and the earnings/Fed calendar rather than a clear retail signal.
